name: No Platform Has Solved It
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Five Approaches, Zero Winners So Far
lesson.summary: Superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, photonic, and topological qubits each trade one hard problem for another, and none has yet demonstrated the combination of scale, fidelity, and connectivity that fault tolerance requires.
lesson.body:
If the barrier ahead were purely a matter of picking the right underlying technology, it would be reasonable to expect one platform to have pulled ahead by now. Instead, several genuinely different physical approaches to building qubits are being pursued in parallel, each with real advantages and real unsolved problems, and none of them has yet demonstrated the combination of qubit count, gate fidelity, and connectivity that fault-tolerant, million-qubit-scale computing requires.

Superconducting qubits, used by IBM and Google among others, are fast and can be fabricated using techniques adapted from the classical chip industry, but they require dilution refrigerators cooling the chip to a small fraction of a degree above absolute zero, and their coherence times, how long a qubit can hold its quantum state before decohering, are measured in tens to hundreds of microseconds, short enough that error correction has to work continuously and fast. Trapped-ion qubits, pursued by companies like IonQ and Quantinuum, tend to have longer coherence times and very high gate fidelities, but their gates are slower, and scaling a single chain of trapped ions to large numbers runs into its own limits, which is why leading groups shuttle ions between multiple small trap zones rather than building one enormous chain.

Neutral-atom platforms, from companies like QuEra and Atom Computing, use laser-controlled optical tweezers to arrange and rearrange atoms, offering a promising path to large qubit counts and reconfigurable layouts, but gate fidelities and fast, reliable mid-circuit measurement, needed continuously for error correction, are still catching up to the other platforms. Photonic approaches, pursued by companies like PsiQuantum, avoid the need for deep cryogenic cooling of the qubits themselves, but photon loss and the probabilistic nature of photonic gates create a different set of hard engineering problems. Topological qubits, Microsoft's long-term bet, are attractive in theory because they would be intrinsically more resistant to errors, reducing the physical-to-logical overhead described earlier in this chapter, but the underlying physical evidence for a working topological qubit has been genuinely contested within the physics community, including at least one earlier claim that had to be walked back after independent scrutiny.

The honest summary is that this is an open, multi-front engineering race, not a solved problem waiting for adoption. Each platform trades one obstacle for another: speed for coherence, fidelity for scalability, simplicity of cooling for difficulty of control. That no platform has solved the full package is itself informative. It suggests the barrier is not a quirk of one particular technology choice but a genuine, cross-cutting engineering challenge that any winning approach will eventually have to overcome.
